name: Benjamin Franklin
role: American printer, scientist and statesman; Pennsylvania Assembly member, colonial agent, diplomat and delegate to the Constitutional Convention (1706-1790)
summary: Franklin was an Enlightenment republican who defended the colonists' right to representation, helped found the United States and favoured a broad franchise, a weak executive and no hereditary honours. He held that poor relief breeds idleness and that trade should be free, yet also that property beyond subsistence is a creature of public law. His slavery views changed from owning slaves to presiding over the Pennsylvania Abolition Society, and his religion was a practical deism.

sources.usedFor: Slaveholding and later abolitionism, German immigration remarks, Declaration and Constitution.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Wrote that trade finds its own rates and that government cannot well interfere in the prices of commodities; mocked export bans and mob price-setting in the Price of Corn essay (1766). Also praised freedom of commerce as a right of all mankind.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Inferred: from his view that superfluous property is the public's to dispose of by law, and from his long fight to have the Penn family's estates taxed like others in the Assembly; no stated call for higher rates on the wealthy.

property-fundamental.rationale: Wrote to Robert Morris (1783) that all property beyond what is needed for subsistence is the creature of public convention, which the public may regulate, limit and dispose of by law; only necessary property is a natural right.

cut-welfare.rationale: In the 1766 and 1768 essays argued that the English poor law gave the poor a dependence besides industry and frugality, 'offered a premium for the encouragement of idleness', increased poverty and should be repealed.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Inferred: argued that freedom of speech is a pillar of free government and that no magistrate can be trusted with power to punish words, though he held abuse of it should be repressed; hate speech was not addressed.

strong-leader.rationale: Inferred: feared that the new government could end in monarchy, advised moderate executive salaries and opposed an absolute presidential veto in 1787.

state-harmful.rationale: Wrote in 1787 'I think a general Government necessary for us' and, in 1783, that those who dislike civil society on its terms may live among savages.

decide-locally.rationale: At the Convention supported a general national government, and wrote that the danger was 'defect of obedience in the subjects'; proposed the Albany colonial union (1754).

more-religion-public.rationale: Moved on 28 June 1787 that the Convention open each day with prayer, saying God governs in the affairs of men; he also gave money to all sects. Motion rejected.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: As Abolition Society president (1789) he endorsed a plan to educate, employ and qualify freed people for civil liberty, calling it a duty.

reduce-immigration.rationale: In 1782 wrote that strangers are welcome in America because there is room for all and old inhabitants are not jealous. His 1751 essay had wanted to limit German influx.

free-trade.rationale: Held that trade should take its own course, called freedom of commerce 'the right of all mankind', and opposed British restraints on colonial and Irish trade; scholars place him in the free-trade, physiocratic camp after c.1767.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Wrote to Rev. John Lathrop (1788) of the 'growing felicity of mankind' from improvements in philosophy, morals, politics and the conveniences of life, expecting medicine to improve similarly.

revolution-justified.rationale: Helped draft and signed the Declaration of Independence and served the Revolution as diplomat; supported impeachment as the alternative to revolution.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Inferred: from his statement that the public has the right of regulating descents and conveyances of property and limiting the quantity and uses of it; he named no inheritance tax.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: In 1747 opposed a colony's import duty as a tax on the consumer and a spur to smuggling, and mocked export prohibitions in 1766. His 1751 essay and 1768 letter had noted that prohibitions on foreign manufactures benefit home labour, so the later view is used.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Praised America's 'general happy mediocrity', with few great proprietors and most people cultivating their own land or following a handicraft, and held that cheap land lets labourers become owners.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Said in 1787 no form of government but may be a blessing if well administered, yet feared monarchy and opposed hereditary rule.

political-violence-never.rationale: Supported the American armed rebellion and voluntary militias for defence, while condemning mob violence and the Paxton massacre of Indians.

war-builds-character.rationale: Wrote in 1783 that 'there never was a good War, or a bad Peace', and lamented war's waste of money and workers' lives.

ethnic-nation.rationale: In 1751 objected that German immigrants would 'Germanize' Pennsylvania and keep their own language, but in 1782 wrote that strangers of any origin are welcome in America. Points both ways.

taxation-theft.rationale: Called the unwillingness to pay taxes blameworthy; money justly due from the people is the creditor's, and those who withhold it should be compelled by law; those who will not 'pay his club' have no right to the benefits of society.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Wrote in 1751 of the importance of securing room for English settlement and of the prince who acquires vacant territory as father of his nation, but condemned wars of conquest in 1785.

national-self-determination.rationale: Signed the Declaration of Independence and argued the colonies' right to govern themselves in their own legislatures rather than by Parliament.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Inferred: from his view that public provision for the poor removes the inducement to work and that the poor should be 'led or driven out' of poverty; he proposed no explicit work requirement.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: In 1751 asked why German settlers should keep their language and customs rather than adopt English ones; he later reportedly softened this view.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Led public projects funded by taxes or subscription (paving and lighting, a paid watch, library, hospital, academy) and favoured a general government; no stated limit to defence, justice and property.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: As president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society signed the 1789 address and the 1790 memorial against slavery; condemned killing Indians for their skin colour (1764); wrote that the poor man has an equal right to representation. His 1751 essay and earlier slaveholding are earlier, now repudiated views.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Wrote that liberty consists in an actual share in appointing lawmakers and that those without a vote are enslaved; argued against Parliament taxing colonists without representation (1766) and that 'rulers are the servants, and the people their superiors and sovereigns'.

trade-surplus.rationale: Wrote in 1768 that without exporting more than a nation imports it could have no money, and in 1751 called laws encouraging exports and discouraging luxury imports 'generative laws'. Later he favoured free trade, so this is mixed.

separated-powers.rationale: A scholar notes he was reluctant to sanction the principle of checks and balances and feared a strong executive, while accepting the Constitution's design.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: In 1751 worried that herding together of German immigrants would exclude English language and manners; he later welcomed strangers of every origin, so contested.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: In the 1766 Price of Corn essay (written as a farmer persona, in earnest) attacked the ban on corn exports and the mob's forced low prices; later wrote that it is contrary to the nature of commerce for government to interfere in prices.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Wrote in 1782 that one or two years' residence gives a stranger all rights of a citizen and opposed a fourteen-year residence requirement at the 1787 Convention, thinking four years enough.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Inferred: from his approval of the Pennsylvania rule that no office should be so profitable as to be desirable and his preference for moderate executive salaries.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: In An Apology for Printers (1731) held that opinions differ and that both sides should be heard, and that printers should print what people wish to read; opposed punishing words.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: At the 1787 Convention approved a seven-year presidential term with no second term, saying there is nothing degrading in the magistrate returning to the mass of the people.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Called agriculture 'the only honest way' to wealth (war is robbery, commerce 'generally cheating') and honoured the husbandman; Americans hold the husbandman in honour.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: In 'Remarks concerning the Savages of North America' wrote that Native Americans' manners differ from ours and each side thinks its own the perfection of civility; found no people wholly rude or wholly polite.

death-penalty.rationale: Opposed death for theft (1785) but wrote that murder may rightly be punished with death; he addressed no case like terrorism.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Stated in the same 1783 letter that property superfluous to subsistence belongs to the public, which created it by its laws and may dispose of it whenever the public welfare desires.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Held that rulers must be accountable; strongly favoured impeachment of the President (1787) so that the head of government can be lawfully called to account.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: In his 1784 letter on the Society of the Cincinnati called descending honours 'groundless and absurd', objected to hereditary knights and entailed estates, and said Americans ask 'What can he do?' not 'What is he?'.

public-money-creation.rationale: Argued in A Modest Enquiry (1729) for the province's issue of paper currency, and later defended colonial legislatures' paper money against Parliament's ban; proposed a moderate public emission or a bank.

elective-rulers.rationale: Held rulers are servants of the people, wrote that those governed by others' choice are enslaved, and opposed hereditary orders.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Signed the Declaration of Independence and in 1787 favoured impeachment, saying without it 'the people have no recourse against oppression but revolution and assassination'.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: In the Pennsylvania Assembly he defended its exclusive right to originate and control money bills against the governor's amendments, and in 1787 proposed that money bills originate in the lower house.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: In 1784 wrote that luxury is not always so great an evil as represented, may spur industry, and cannot be prevented by law; earlier (1751) said luxury should never be allowed to become common. Mature view used; mixed.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: His 'Rules by Which a Great Empire May Be Reduced to a Small One' (1773, satire) and the Stamp Act examination argue colonies should share equal rights and not be governed in the interest of the mother country; 1751 essay called restraints on colonial manufactures unwise.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Argued in 1784 that honour should not descend to posterity and opposed hereditary orders; in 1787 feared the government might end in monarchy.

property-franchise.rationale: At the 1787 Convention opposed limiting the vote to freeholders, saying common people's virtue and public spirit must not be depressed; wrote that those with no vote are enslaved.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Inferred: argued that slavery let a few families acquire vast estates while the poor lost employment, that laws made by the rich to protect their property began a tyranny, and warned the 1787 Convention against partiality to the rich.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Contrasted the compulsory poor-rate, which he held harmful, with the voluntary hospitals and almshouses maintained by charity, which he praised, and held that the best help to the poor is to lead them out of poverty rather than make them easy in it.

term-limits.rationale: Approved the draft article barring a second presidential term (1787); did not address terms in other offices.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Ridiculed gentlemen 'doing nothing of value, but living idly on the Labour of others' (the 'Gentleman-Hog') and said Americans honour useful work, not birth, in 'Information to Those Who Would Remove to America'.

second-chamber.rationale: Preferred a single legislative body (the Pennsylvania model); in 1789 argued that a single house stifles bad motions early and that two houses cause delay, although he accepted the Convention's compromise creating two.

racial-pride.rationale: In 1751 wrote he wished the numbers of 'purely white' English and Saxons increased and that his partiality to his country's complexion is natural to mankind. Not restated later; his later writings reject colour distinctions.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Wrote in 1785 that a nation making an unjust war is 'a great gang' of robbers and in 1783 that there never was a good war; he nonetheless urged taking Canada in peace talks, so not absolute.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Wrote to Ezra Stiles (1790) that belief in one God, providence, worship, doing good to others and an immortal soul are the fundamental principles of all sound religion, which he regarded alike in whatever sect.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: In 1751 objected that German settlers would never adopt English language or customs; not restated later and he reportedly reconsidered.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Wrote that at fifteen he began to doubt revelation and became a 'thorough Deist'; later wrote that revelation had no weight with him as such, and doubted Jesus's divinity in his 1790 letter to Ezra Stiles.

notes: Slavery: Franklin owned slaves and printed advertisements for their sale; by the late 1750s he argued against slavery and in 1787-1790 was president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society. His 1790 'Sidi Mehemet Ibrahim' piece is a parody that voices the pro-slavery argument in order to refute it; it is read as supporting abolition. The 1751 Increase of Mankind essay contains remarks on German immigrants and 'purely white' people that later printings dropped; immigration answers use the mature position or are left low. Answers marked Inferred rely on stated views only.
